name: ai-vocabulary
title: Vocabulary of machine-written prose
description:
AI writing draws on a recognisable vocabulary. This set holds one rule that measures how much of it a document uses.

A register is a way of writing rather than a thing written about — academic, tabloid, legal, chatty are registers, and so is the way a machine writes a pull request description. A word list is only about the writing if the subject is held still, and holding it still is what the derivation below spends its effort on.

The words are derived here rather than taken from anyone. Some public pull request descriptions sign themselves — a trailing attribution line, or a shouted HTML comment. That signature says one thing reliably: this description was written by a machine. It does not say the unsigned ones were written by people, and it does not say a group holding more signatures is more machine-sounding, so it is used in exactly one place.

tools/pr-sample.mjs samples a day of descriptions each morning and keeps each as a bag of words. tools/pr-cluster.mjs then does three things. It clusters coarsely and takes the group with the largest signed share, which is the register — that is the one use of the signature. It ranks that group's vocabulary by how much more the group uses each word than the whole rest of the corpus does. And it clusters again finely, dropping any word common enough to measure inside a single stratum and nowhere else, because such a word belongs to one part of the register rather than to the register.

The middle step is what makes the list usable. Ranking by how much more the signed half uses a word finds the work rather than the writing — agents get pointed at typecheck failures, so that vocabulary comes back, with a tool's own name at the top — and it has no term for rarity, so ordinary words outrank distinctive ones. Contrasting the register against the whole corpus supplies both. Measured on data/corpus, ranking by the signature alone catches 9 of 24 machine-written documents; ranking by the contrast catches 20.

It rebuilds itself: the sample runs daily, the derivation weekly. The agent signatures it splits on are groomed by hand through a pull request, because which tools exist is the one part that goes out of date on its own.

rules.name: Vocabulary shared with machine-written prose
rules.description: How many different words from the list a document uses. No single word is a tell, and the list holds ordinary ones; it is the spread across the list that fires the rule.
rules.suggest: No one word here is wrong, so do not walk the list swapping them out. The finding names every word that counted: rewrite the passages carrying the most of them, in words you would have chosen yourself, until the rate falls.
rules.note: Each word counts once however often it appears, so a document that genuinely needs one pays for it once and only breadth accumulates. The total is divided by the square root of the length rather than by the length, because a count of distinct things saturates as a document grows. The list is derived from pull request descriptions and carries that shape: a word may be characteristic of machine-written software prose without being characteristic of machine-written prose in general. data/corpus holds twenty-four matched pairs of general prose — one topic written twice, once by a person before these tools existed and once by a model — which is what this rule is measured against before any change to it ships.

hit:
The proposal rests on a premise nobody has stated plainly, and the review board should say so before it votes. The claim is that the current interface carries the whole of the scheduling behaviour, and that replacing it is therefore a contained change. That claim was asserted rather than measured. When the timings were finally taken, the picture that survived was the opposite of the one in the summary: the interface handles about a third of the work, and the remainder sits in two helpers that nobody has touched since the fourth release.

Two halves of the migration were handed to different teams, and neither half settles the question alone. The first team drew a boundary at the queue and stopped. The second team assumed the boundary was elsewhere and built against it. Both were working honestly from the same document, which quietly leaves the seam undefined. The disagreement between them is load-bearing, and papering over it in the status report is worse than leaving it open, because a reader now believes a question was settled that was never asked.

What is owed to the reviewers is a plain account of what is known. Eleven of the fourteen benchmarks were re-measured after the change and came back within noise of the numbers taken before it. Two got worse, by amounts that are small but consistent across repeated runs. The last one was refused outright by the harness and has not been investigated. Nothing in the write-up mentions the refusal, and the summary table shows thirteen rows where there should be fourteen.

The ceiling the design sets is narrower than the machinery beneath it can honour. That is not a defect in the implementation; it is a decision that was made early, deliberately, and for reasons that were good at the time and have gone stale since. Whoever revisits it should know that the constraint predates the current traffic pattern by three years. The asymmetry it introduces between reads and writes is genuine, and it will not be argued away.

None of this makes the migration a bad idea. It makes the estimate wrong. The work that stands between here and a shipped change is roughly twice what the plan admits, and the plan gains nothing by holding the smaller figure. A revised estimate that is honest about the two helpers, the undefined seam and the refused benchmark is worth more to the people deciding than a confident one that quietly omits them. The reviewers can then judge the trade for themselves, which is what they are there for, and the decision that follows will rest on something that holds.

The schedule attached to the proposal assumes the review completes in a single round. Reviews of this size have taken two or three rounds in each of the last four quarters, and there is no reason to expect this one to behave differently. Adding a second round moves the delivery date into the following quarter, which changes who has to be told and when. That is a conversation to have now rather than in six weeks.

There is a version of this change that is genuinely contained, and it is worth describing because it may be the right one. Leave the two helpers where they are, move only the queue boundary, and accept that the seam stays undefined for another release. That version is smaller than the one on the table, it carries less risk, and it does not require the estimate to be revised. What it does not do is deliver the throughput number the proposal opens with, and the reviewers should be told that plainly rather than discovering it in the following quarter's report when the number has quietly moved.

None of the three reviewers has asked for the raw timings, and the raw timings are where the disagreement lives. They should be attached to the next revision whether or not anybody asks, because a reader who wants to check the claim currently cannot, and a claim that cannot be checked is worth less than one that is simply stated without numbers at all.

rules.evidence: At 3.8 distinct list words per root word: 0 of 24 human documents and 20 of 24 machine documents in data/corpus. The threshold sits above every human document in that corpus with a margin rather than on the highest one (3.69), because twenty-four documents cannot resolve a boundary more finely than that; sitting on the maximum would read 21 of 24 and be worth less than it looks. rules/load-bearing.json reaches 22 of 24 at one false alarm and ties this at 21 when no false alarm is allowed. Before the derivation was changed to rank against the rest of the corpus rather than against the unsigned half, the same pipeline reached 9 of 24; see docs/vocabulary.md for why.

$comment: Off, and in candidates/, until it beats rules/load-bearing.json on data/corpus. The derivation and the page are the point for now; the rule ships when it wins.
